```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("_setup.R")
library(bayesmokken)
```

```{r fit, include = FALSE}
data(srs)
emp <- mokken_h(srs, warn = FALSE)
fit <- bb_mokken_h(srs, draws = 2000, seed = 1)
```

This vignette defines what the package estimates. Nearby executable chunks are
labelled by what they actually establish:

- **Independent oracle** — a separate implementation starts from raw inputs.
- **Metamorphic/invariant check** — a transformation that should preserve a
  result is exercised.
- **Executable consistency check/illustration** — returned fields are combined
  according to the displayed identity, catching documentation or wiring drift
  without claiming an independent derivation.

The three coefficient checks below are independent oracles: they recompute the
moments from the raw response matrix and never read a covariance, denominator
or coefficient back out of the fitted object. The transport and HBB vignettes
carry the other two oracles.

## Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $F$ | the population distribution of responses |
| $S = \{1, \dots, J\}$ | the **declared** item set, fixed in advance |
| $Y_i$ | response to item $i$ |
| $p_i$ | mean of $Y_i$ (for binary items, the proportion endorsing) |
| $H_{ij}$ | pair scalability coefficient |
| $H_i$ | item scalability coefficient |
| $H$ | scale scalability coefficient |
| $n$ | number of complete-scale respondents |
| $G$ | number of clusters |
| $n_g$ | number of respondents in cluster $g$ |

The symbols match the two articles. Vignettes m2 through m5 use them without
redefinition.

## The three coefficients

The scalability coefficient is a ratio of a covariance to the largest
covariance those marginals permit [@loevinger1948; @mokken1971]. For a pair,

$$H_{ij} = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y_i, Y_j)}{\operatorname{Cov}^{\max}(Y_i, Y_j)}.$$

**Independent oracle — recompute every pair from the raw response matrix.**
Nothing below reads a coefficient, covariance or denominator from the fitted
object; the moments come from the matrix and the binary maximum covariance from
its closed form, $\operatorname{Cov}^{\max} = \min(p_i, p_j) - p_i p_j$.

```{r verify-pair}
p <- bm_pair_h(emp)

X <- as.matrix(srs[stats::complete.cases(srs), ])
mu <- colMeans(X)

oracle <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(p)), function(k) {
  i <- as.character(p$item_i[k])
  j <- as.character(p$item_j[k])
  cov_ij <- mean(X[, i] * X[, j]) - mu[[i]] * mu[[j]]
  max_ij <- min(mu[[i]], mu[[j]]) - mu[[i]] * mu[[j]]
  c(covariance = cov_ij, max_covariance = max_ij, H = cov_ij / max_ij)
}, numeric(3)))

stopifnot(
  max(abs(oracle[, "covariance"]     - p$covariance))     < 1e-12,
  max(abs(oracle[, "max_covariance"] - p$max_covariance)) < 1e-12,
  max(abs(oracle[, "H"]              - p$H))              < 1e-12
)
data.frame(pairs_checked = nrow(p),
           max_absolute_difference = max(abs(oracle[, "H"] - p$H)))
```

For an item and for the scale, the coefficients are ratios of **sums**:

$$H_i = \frac{\sum_{j \neq i} \operatorname{Cov}(Y_i, Y_j)}{\sum_{j \neq i} \operatorname{Cov}^{\max}(Y_i, Y_j)},
\qquad
H = \frac{\sum_{i < j} \operatorname{Cov}(Y_i, Y_j)}{\sum_{i < j} \operatorname{Cov}^{\max}(Y_i, Y_j)}.$$

**Independent oracle — aggregate the oracle's own pair moments.** The sums
below come from the matrix-derived quantities above, not from the fitted
object's columns, so agreement is a check rather than an identity.

```{r verify-scale}
stopifnot(all.equal(
  bm_scale_h(emp)$H,
  sum(oracle[, "covariance"]) / sum(oracle[, "max_covariance"]),
  tolerance = 1e-12
))
data.frame(package = bm_scale_h(emp)$H,
           oracle  = sum(oracle[, "covariance"]) / sum(oracle[, "max_covariance"]))
```

### A ratio of sums is not a mean of ratios

This is the single most common misreading, so it is worth making concrete
rather than merely stating:

```{r ratio-vs-mean}
c(ratio_of_sums = sum(p$covariance) / sum(p$max_covariance),
  mean_of_pair_H = mean(p$H))
```

The two differ by `r fmt_h(abs(sum(p$covariance)/sum(p$max_covariance) - mean(p$H)), 4)`
on these data — not a rounding discrepancy but a different quantity. Averaging
the pair coefficients would weight every pair equally regardless of how much
covariance it can carry. The ratio of sums lets pairs with more room to
covary count for more, which is what the coefficient is defined to do.

The same applies at the item level:

**Independent oracle — every item, from the oracle's pair moments.** The
earlier version of this chunk checked one item against the fitted object's own
columns. It now aggregates the matrix-derived moments, for all eleven items.

```{r verify-item}
items <- bm_item_h(emp)
oracle_item <- vapply(items$item, function(it) {
  own <- p$item_i == it | p$item_j == it
  sum(oracle[own, "covariance"]) / sum(oracle[own, "max_covariance"])
}, numeric(1))

stopifnot(max(abs(oracle_item - items$H)) < 1e-12)
data.frame(items_checked = length(oracle_item),
           max_absolute_difference = max(abs(oracle_item - items$H)))
```

## The estimand is a fixed, declared scale

$S$ is fixed before the data are seen. The package estimates the coefficient
**of that set**, and its interval covers sampling variation in the responses
only.

It does **not** propagate uncertainty from having chosen the items. If you
select items by inspecting these data — dropping the two weakest, say — the
selection is itself an estimated quantity, and an interval that ignores it is
too narrow by an amount this package does not attempt to quantify. Automatic
item selection procedures exist in the wider literature
[@van_der_ark_mokken_2008]; nothing here performs one, and no interval reported
here should be attached to a scale that was chosen by looking.

The practical consequence is a rule you can apply: **an interval belongs to the
item set that was declared when it was computed.** `bm_compare()` enforces this
by refusing to align fits whose item sets differ unless you pass
`allow_different = TRUE`.

```{r fixed-scale}
bm_provenance(fit)$item_set_hash
```

That hash is what makes the declaration checkable after the fact.

## The row target: complete-scale respondents

The second half of the estimand is *which respondents*.

```{r rows}
c(rows_in_data = nrow(srs), complete_scale = bm_interval(fit)$n_complete)
```

Under the default `missing = "complete_scale"`, a respondent enters only if
they answered every item in $S$. This is part of the estimand, not a
preprocessing convenience: the coefficient is defined over the population of
respondents who would answer the whole scale, and a different missing-data rule
defines a different population.

`bm_check_data()` reports the count before you fit, and `n_complete` records it
in the result. For clustered fits, `n_complete` counts **respondents**;
the cluster count is a separate field.

```{r clustered-fields}
cl <- bm_interval(bm_cached("cwb_respondent"))
c(respondents = cl$n_complete, clusters = cl$cluster_count,
  calibration_input = cl$calibration_n)
```

## Weights

`weights` supplies a fixed, known weight per respondent — a survey design
weight, typically. Weights are normalised internally, so only their relative
sizes matter, and they enter the covariance and its maximum alike:

```{r weights}
w <- rep(c(1, 2), length.out = nrow(srs))
h_w <- mokken_h(srs, weights = w, warn = FALSE)
c(unweighted = bm_scale_h(emp)$H, weighted = bm_scale_h(h_w)$H)
```

These are fixed weights, not the random weights of the Bayesian bootstrap.
`vignette("m2-bayesian-bootstrap-calibration")` covers the latter, and
`vignette("m4-hierarchical-bb-targets")` covers the cluster weighting that
defines the two population targets.

## Boundaries: when the denominator vanishes

$H$ is a ratio, so it is undefined when its denominator is zero, and unstable
when the denominator is merely very small. Two items that are nearly constant,
or whose marginals leave almost no room to covary, produce exactly that.

The package does not hide these cases. Every level of the result carries a
`denominator_status`:

```{r denominator}
table(bm_pair_h(emp)$denominator_status)
bm_scale_h(emp)$denominator_status
```

Two tolerances govern the handling. `zero_tol` sets the point below which a
denominator counts as zero rather than small. `eta` sets the point below which
a pair is flagged as near-boundary while still being computed. Both are
arguments with documented defaults, and both are recorded in the result, so a
reader can tell what was treated how.

```{r tolerances}
emp$tolerances
```

Near-boundary pairs are **reported, not dropped**. Dropping them would change
the estimand — the sums in the numerator and denominator would run over a
different set of pairs — without saying so in the output. Flagging them leaves
the choice with you.

Within a bootstrap, a draw whose denominator vanishes yields an undefined
coefficient. Those draws are counted rather than quietly discarded:

```{r defined-draws}
iv <- bm_interval(fit)
c(defined = iv$defined_draws, total = iv$total_draws,
  minimum_required = iv$minimum_defined_draws)
```

If too few draws are defined the interval fails rather than being computed from
whatever survived. `vignette("m2-bayesian-bootstrap-calibration")` gives the
minima.
